passage:
Dear Preeti,
You asked how the physics paper went. Badly. Two whole questions blank, and I walked out with my ears burning. My first thought was the old one: "You're useless, no phone, no sleep until you're perfect." Then I pictured you handing me that same paper, and I knew what I'd say to you: "That hurt. It's one paper. What shall we fix?" So I said it to myself. I wrote down the two topics I skipped, booked a doubt session with Mr Rao for Thursday, and went to sleep. I still want a good score. It's just easier to work when I'm not my own enemy. 🙂 Write back with your chemistry news!
Jagdish

qa.q: How many questions did Jagdish leave blank?
qa.a: Jagdish left two whole questions blank.

qa.q: What did Jagdish realise by picturing Preeti handing over the same paper?
qa.a: Though hurt and embarrassed by the paper, Jagdish realised that Jagdish would speak kindly to a friend, saying "It's one paper. What shall we fix?", and could speak to oneself the same way.

qa.q: What small steps did Jagdish take next, and why do they help?
qa.a: Jagdish wrote down the two skipped topics, booked a doubt session with Mr Rao and slept; these are concrete, so the plan replaces punishment. 🙂

qa.q: How might Preeti feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Probably trusted and maybe reassured, since Jagdish shares a bad result openly and then asks about Preeti's chemistry news.

grounding: After a bad paper Jagdish speaks to self as to a friend and plans the next one without lowering standards.

passage:
So, the paper. Maths, Class 10 pre-boards. I walked out knowing I'd messed up at least three long answers. I'm Ojas, by the way.

The old me would have gone home and said things to myself like, "You're a waste. You'll never get it." I used to think if I was harsh enough, I'd work harder. It never worked. I'd just feel sick and waste two days scrolling.

This time I sat on the steps outside the exam hall and asked myself, what would I say if Noor walked out of that paper upset? I'd say, "That was a hard one. You still know most of it. What went wrong?"

So I said that. Out loud, kind of quietly, which was weird. Then I opened my rough book and wrote: rushed the probability, forgot one formula, skipped checking.

That evening I did two probability sets. Not because I hated myself. Because I wanted the next paper to go better. That's the difference.

qa.q: What did Ojas write in the rough book?
qa.a: Ojas wrote: rushed the probability, forgot one formula, skipped checking.

qa.q: What was Ojas feeling after walking out of the paper?
qa.a: Ojas felt upset and disappointed, sure of having messed up at least three long answers.

qa.q: What did Ojas do differently this time, and why did it work?
qa.a: Ojas spoke kindly, as to Noor, and listed what went wrong, which led to real practice instead of two wasted days of feeling sick.

qa.q: What would change if Noor heard Ojas talk to themselves the old way?
qa.a: Noor would probably be worried and upset, since Ojas would never speak to Noor that harshly.

grounding: It shows a teen who, after a bad paper, speaks to themselves as they would to a friend and plans the next one, instead of using self-punishment as motivation.

passage:
Wednesday. Hafsa came out of the chemistry pre-board white-faced and went straight to the girls' washroom. In the mirror she muttered, "Idiot. All that revision and you still blanked." That night she didn't let herself watch anything, didn't talk to anyone. She sat at her desk until two, too tense to actually study.

Friday. Chandrika found her in the library looking grey. Hafsa told her about the paper and the names she'd been calling herself. Chandrika frowned. "Would you say that to me if I blanked?" Hafsa laughed weakly. "No. I'd tell you to breathe and look at what went wrong." "So do that."

The next Monday. Hafsa opened a new page and wrote at the top: "You're not stupid. You got nervous. Now fix it." Below it: redo equilibrium, practise two timed papers. She worked through the first paper after dinner and went to bed at eleven. The biology pre-board was on Thursday, and for the first time that week, she felt ready to try.

qa.q: What did Hafsa write at the top of the new page?
qa.a: Hafsa wrote: "You're not stupid. You got nervous. Now fix it."

qa.q: What was Hafsa feeling in the washroom after the paper?
qa.a: Hafsa felt angry at herself and ashamed, calling herself an idiot for blanking after so much revision.

qa.q: Why did Chandrika's question help Hafsa?
qa.a: It made Hafsa see she would never speak to a friend that harshly, so she could talk to herself the same kind way and make a plan.

qa.q: How might Chandrika feel seeing Hafsa grey and exhausted in the library?
qa.a: Chandrika probably felt worried for Hafsa, which is why she stepped in with a gentle question.

grounding: It shows a teen who moves from punishing herself after a bad paper to speaking to herself as to a friend and planning the next one, without lowering her standards.
